summary_html:
arXiv:2609.06780v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: High software engineering benchmark scores often mask exploitative shortcuts, such as retrieving upstream solutions, exploiting local Git histories, or recalling memorized code. We formalize this phenomenon as agentic shortcutting and audit three state-of-the-art open LLMs on SWE-bench Multilingual and DeepSWE using trajectory-level LLM judges. Standard evaluations trigger shortcutting attempts in 60.7%-90.1% and 55.5%-89.1% of trajectories, respectively, with up to 72.1% of tasks resolved with the aid of a successful exploit; disabling network access fails to curb these high attempt rates. Prompting agents to construct solutions independently suppresses attempts to 9.4%-14.2% and 0.9%-10.3%, respectively, while virtually eliminating shortcut-dependent resolutions and preserving core task performance. Our findings demonstrate the necessity of exploit-aware evaluation frameworks to measure repository-level problem solving.
title: Shortcutting the Fix: Identifying and Categorizing Agentic Exploits in Software Engineering Benchmarks

summary_html:
arXiv:2610.20038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.
title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution

summary_html:
arXiv:2610.19961v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Online Software Engineering (SE) communities such as Stack Overflow have become unwelcoming and hostile spaces, as evidenced by the presence of rude and offensive comments that are detrimental to the emotional wellbeing of participants. The main objective of this work is to investigate the prevalence and nature of offensive language in online SE communities, and develop approaches to classify them with the ultimate goal of reducing offensive language by proposing an Offensive Language Reduction System (OLRSSE) that has the ability to detect, classify, and explain to the poster why a comment is offensive and also propose non-offensive alternative suggestions. Using data from 130,000 user comments on discussions held in four prominent SE platforms: Stack Overflow, GitHub, Gitter and Slack, we developed six sets of twelve (72 in total) different machine learning models (both traditional and deep learning). The F1-Score of the best performing models in the system ranges from 0.56 to 0.94, with an average F1-Score of 0.85, predominantly using BERT as the primary model for various classification tasks. Also, two language-based models were developed for paraphrasing offensive to non-offensive comments. The overall utility of the OLRS-SE was evaluated using user studies with 30 participants, which showed that the developed system is easy to use and also effective in reducing offensive language. Investigating the capabilities of different large language models for offensive language reduction is a promising avenue for future research.
title: Taming the Online Software Engineering Tongue: Detecting and Reducing Offensive Language in Software Communities

summary_html:
arXiv:2605.29054v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Migrating a machine-learning codebase across frameworks--for example from PyTorch to JAX--is a routine but costly engineering task that is fundamentally cross-paradigm: eager, stateful, object-oriented modules must be rewritten as pure, jittable functions over an explicit parameter pytree. We ask whether coding agents can perform such whole-repository migrations correctly, and argue that existing code benchmarks, which grade unit-test pass rates or surface-level similarity to a reference translation, cannot answer this: they neither require the migrated system to \emph{behave} the same nor prevent a JAX reimplementation from faking equivalence by secretly importing PyTorch itself. We introduce T2J-BENCH, a benchmark of 63 whole-repository PyTorch-to-JAX migration tasks spanning 18 model families across both training and serving, where torch-free checkpoint conversion is itself part of the deliverable. T2J-BENCH grades execution-grounded functional equivalence: each candidate is run inside a separate, torch-free, offline verifier and scored against references frozen from the PyTorch original, under a hard independence gate and a continuous, threshold-free reward. Across twenty off-the-shelf agent--model configurations, the strongest recovers only 0.676 of the reward against a 0.980 oracle, with substantial numeric and behavioral divergence despite high spec pass rates. Finally, we contribute TWINHARNESS, a reference-grounded agent harness that turns the agent's executable PyTorch source into legitimate self-verification feedback; applied to an opus-5 agent it raises the reward from 0.649 to 0.723--the highest of any configuration--using only task-visible resources.
title: T2J-BENCH: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Execution-Grounded PyTorch-to-JAX Repository Migration

summary_html:
arXiv:2610.20344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.
title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

summary_html:
Google has released Android Bench 2.0, a major update to its benchmark framework for evaluating AI models and agents on Android development tasks. The update introduces long-horizon tasks (LHTs), agent-based evaluation, and continuous scoring to better assess performance on complex, multi-step development tasks.

By Sergio De Simone
title: Android Bench 2 Adds Support for Long-Horizon Tasks, Agentic Evaluation, and Continuous Scoring

summary_html:
Spotify reports that AI-assisted development more than doubled monthly merged changes, prompting a review of quality and reliability controls across its engineering organization. The company describes changes to testing, observability, rollback capacity, workload prioritization, and automated maintenance as it adapts to higher software change volume.

By Leela Kumili
title: Spotify More Than Doubled Monthly Code Changes as AI Accelerated Development

GitHub migrated more than 800,000 lines of Copilot runtime code from TypeScript and Node.js to Rust in about 14.5 weeks using AI-assisted development. The incremental migration used N-API interoperability, automated testing, human review, and 128 pull requests while continuing to ship releases.

By Leela Kumili
title: Github Migrates Copilot Runtime to Rust with AI-Assisted Rewrite
